The government should absolutely pursue decriminalizing the personal use of recreational drugs. Criminalizing drug use has proven to be a failed policy that disproportionately harms marginalized communities, fuels mass incarceration, and does little to address addiction as a public health issue. Decriminalization shifts the focus from punishment to harm reduction, allowing resources to be redirected toward education, treatment, and social services that actually help individuals struggling with substance abuse.  

Portugal’s successful decriminalization model demonstrates that treating drug use as a health issue—not a criminal one—reduces overdose deaths, lowers HIV transmission rates, and decreases stigma, making people more likely to seek help. Criminalization, on the other hand, drives drug use underground, making it more dangerous and isolating users from support systems.  

My stance is rooted in values of compassion, evidence-based policy, and social justice. Punishing people for personal drug use is morally unjustifiable when the real solutions lie in healthcare and systemic support. Decriminalization is not an endorsement of drug use but an acknowledgment that prohibition has failed. The government must prioritize humane, effective policies over outdated, punitive approaches that only perpetuate harm.
